about: Building materials (roadmap BT3a): Roofs, the coverings (thatch, shingles, stone slates, slate, clay tiles, lead, corrugated iron) and the timber roof structures (crown-post, king-post, queen-post, arch-braced and hammerbeam roofs). Fields as bidb/building_materials.py.

materials.name: Thatch

period.text: about 1000 BC: the Bronze Age roundhouses of Must Farm, Cambridgeshire, whose roofs were found charred in situ 'after 3,000 years' (roundhouses with conical thatched roofs were the standard house of Britain and Ireland from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age); the usual roof of most of the English countryside until the late 1800s; still laid (about 60,000 thatched properties in the UK in 2013)

regions.text: Everywhere in the isles; water reed mainly in East Anglia, straw elsewhere in England, cereal straw over turf on the blackhouses of Lewis

materials.technology: Needs only local vegetation and a light roof frame. Banned for new roofs in London in 1212 after a fire; from 1820 Welsh slate, carried by canals and then railways, gave the countryside other roofs, and thatch declined with the agricultural depression of the late 19th century.
materials.note: Wikipedia notes that no direct evidence of straw thatch survives in Europe before the early medieval period; the Bronze Age date rests on the excavated roofs of Must Farm and on the roundhouses generally.

materials.name: Straw thatch (long straw and combed wheat reed)

period.text: base coats of straw thatch laid over 500 years ago survive on more than 250 roofs in southern England (about 1500 or earlier: the year is a floor, not a first use); still laid with long straw or combed wheat reed

regions.text: Southern England; the medieval base coats are of wheat, rye or maslin

materials.technology: Tall medieval wheat gave grain and long, durable straw. The combine harvester (late 1930s and 1940s), short-stemmed wheats and nitrogen fertiliser made thatching straw scarce and weak; since the 1980s specialist growers raise tall heritage wheats for it.

materials.name: Stone slates (Collyweston, Stonesfield, Horsham, gritstone)

period.text: Roman: Horsham Stone roof slates at the villas of Bignor and Fishbourne (the Fishbourne palace was built about AD 75-80; the year is the palace's, not a dated slate); Stonesfield slate was quarried extensively in the 18th and 19th centuries; Horsham Stone's large-scale extraction stopped by the 1880s; quarries reopened at Nowhurst (2004) and Collyweston (2015) to repair historic roofs

regions.text: Limestone 'slates' of the Jurassic belt (Collyweston in Northamptonshire, Lincolnshire, Rutland and Cambridgeshire; Stonesfield in Oxfordshire), Horsham Stone in Sussex and the Weald, Millstone Grit flags in the Pennines

materials.technology: Fissile beds of limestone and sandstone split into heavy roofing slabs; Collyweston stone was left out for three winters for the frost to open its layers, which artificial freezing has replicated since the late 1990s.

materials.name: Slate

period.text: Roman: the later levels of the fort at Segontium (Caernarfon), founded in AD 77 or 78 and first roofed with tiles, contain many roofing slates (77 is the fort's founding year, so the first slates are somewhat later); small-scale quarrying through the Middle Ages; the boom ran from the abolition of the slate duty in 1831 to Welsh production's peak in 1898; still quarried on a much smaller scale

regions.text: North-west Wales above all; also Cornwall (Delabole), the Lake District (Burlington, Honister), Argyll (Easdale, Ballachulish) and Valentia Island in Kerry

materials.technology: Splits into thin, light, nearly waterproof sheets. A 20% tax on slate carried coastwise (1794-1831) held the trade back; after it was abolished, narrow gauge railways to the ports and then the main lines carried Welsh slate across Britain. Cheaper tiles closed most large quarries in the 1960s and 1970s.

materials.technology: Landowners (Richard Pennant at Penrhyn, Assheton Smith at Dinorwic) took over the quarries in the late 18th century; quarry railways to the ports (Penrhyn 1798, Dinorwic 1824, Ffestiniog Railway 1833-36), slate mills and the Greaves sawing table (1859) made it the cheap roof of industrial Britain.
